title: Moses sees the land (Deuteronomy 34)
hook: on Mount Nebo he sees the land he'll never enter, and dies

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses set two plates before his people: life and death. Your line was choose life. Where was your small fork, and which plate did you pick? Day four hundred nine.

An old man climbs a mountain alone. He's a hundred and twenty years old. Forty of those years he's spent walking a whole people through the desert: through complaints and manna, golden calves and giants, the long funeral march of a generation. And now they're camped by the Jordan River, one crossing away from the land they've been walking toward his entire adult life. But he won't cross. He's been told. So he climbs Mount Nebo, on the east side of the river, and at the top, God shows him everything: the hills to the north, the valleys, the palm-tree city of Jericho, all the way to the sea in the west.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY YEARS OLD.` → `ONE RIVER AWAY.` → `UP NEBO, ALONE.`

segments.voice: Then God says, in the King James Bible: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." Why can't he go? Back in the book of Numbers, at a place called Meribah, Moses struck a rock in anger instead of speaking to it as God told him, and he was told then that he wouldn't lead the people in. Readers have argued for centuries about whether that seems fair. The text doesn't argue. It just tells it. "So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab." And then a mysterious detail: God buried him, in a valley, "but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." No grave to visit. No shrine. The man who led them out is gone, and the people go on without a monument. The chapter adds that "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated." He didn't wear out. He was simply finished. And it ends with an epitaph: there never arose a prophet like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face. Who wrote this chapter, describing Moses' own death? Jewish tradition in the Talmud offers more than one answer: some sages said Joshua wrote the last verses; others said Moses wrote them himself, in tears. Today Mount Nebo is in Jordan, and pilgrims climb it to look out over the same view. Pope John Paul II stood there in the year two thousand. Moses gave his whole life to a promise he saw but didn't enter. Christians remember that he does appear, much later, on another mountain, talking with Jesus at the transfiguration.
screen: `SEE IT, BUT NOT GO OVER.` · `NO MAN KNOWETH HIS GRAVE.` · `HIS EYE WAS NOT DIM.` · `WHO WROTE HIS DEATH?` · then, large: `I HAVE CAUSED THEE TO SEE IT WITH THINE EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a future you won't see. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're working toward that will likely outlast you, or that others will finish. Children or grandchildren. Students. A garden. A business, a church, a cause, a tree you planted. Picture it years from now, flourishing, without you in the picture. Notice what that feels like. Then, like Moses on the mountain, look out over it and let it be enough to have seen it begin. If you pray, you can bless it, and the people who'll carry it on. The bell holds the time.
Moses sees the land. From Mount Nebo, at a hundred and twenty, he sees the promise he gave his life to, and dies before he crosses.
Your line: seeing is enough. Today, do one thing for someone who'll come after you, and don't wait to see how it turns out. Day four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Christian pilgrims visit Mount Nebo in Jordan, where a memorial church stands, and preachers often turn to Deuteronomy 34 at funerals and farewells to speak of work handed on to others.

fork.setup: you're Moses, a hundred and twenty, on top of Nebo. God shows you the whole promised land and says you won't go over. what happens?
options: you plead and are allowed to cross.
you look, and you die there in Moab.
you go down and lead them anyway.
fork.reveal: he sees it all with his own eyes, and dies there in the land of Moab. God buries him, and no one knows where.

original.note: Hebrew: Nebo, the mountain east of the Jordan where Moses saw the land. Today it is in Jordan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad ending.
what it means: a life given to a promise he saw but didn't enter, ending with no grave and an epitaph: no prophet like him.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud debates who wrote Deuteronomy 34, Joshua or Moses in tears; and Nebo looks across to Jericho.

notes: Bava Batra 15a: one view that Joshua wrote the last eight verses; R. Simeon's view that Moses wrote them in tears (or 'with tears'). Paraphrased; confirm.
Pope John Paul II visited Mount Nebo in March 2000; confirm.
Meribah (Numbers 20:7–12): Moses was told to speak to the rock and struck it; the script says 'in anger'. Confirm the characterization.
Deuteronomy 34:6 'he buried him' is often read as God burying Moses; the script says God buried him. Confirm.
